::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Climate models usually read agricultural ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) from a fixed inventory, so nothing the model does can change it. Fung, Val Martin and Tai added an ammonia volatilisation scheme to the land model CLM5 and coupled it to the CAM4-chem atmosphere inside CESM2, so fertiliser ammonia is computed online and two feedbacks can act on it: nitrogen deposited back onto land, and aerosols changing the climate the soil experiences. The model attributes $14\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ of global ammonia emission to fertiliser, above the $9$–$10\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ in common inventories. With $30\%$ more synthetic fertiliser in 2050, emission rises $3.3\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$. The deposition feedback adds $0.47\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ and the aerosol–climate feedback removes $0.41$, and the change in global radiative flux is $-0.005\text{ W m}^{-2}$, which the authors call negligible. Afterwards you should be able to say which loop an offline inventory breaks, what each feedback does, and why their global effects are small.
:::

::: {.callout-note}

An earlier version of this page reported results that are not in the paper it cited: a $42.3\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ flux, a $72\%$ rise in ammonium nitrate, a global forcing of $-0.24\text{ W m}^{-2}$ and $-1.8\text{ W m}^{-2}$ over Asia, CAM6 and the MAM4 aerosol module. The study used CAM4-chem with a bulk aerosol scheme and found a negligible global radiative effect. The page, its figure and its interactive widget, which was built on the same numbers, have been replaced with what the paper reports[^2].
:::

## The loop that offline emissions break

Ammonia from fertilised soil does not stay where it was emitted. Some deposits back onto land, adding nitrogen to soils that then emit more; some forms ammonium aerosol, which changes radiation and therefore the temperature and moisture of the soils that emit it:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    Fert["Synthetic fertiliser"] --> Soil["Soil ammonium (CLM5)"]
    Soil -->|"volatilisation"| NH3["Atmospheric NH3"]
    NH3 -->|"deposition"| Soil
    NH3 -->|"aerosol formation"| Aer["Ammonium aerosol (CAM4-chem)"]
    Aer -->|"radiation and climate"| Clim["Soil temperature and moisture"]
    Clim -->|"controls volatilisation"| Soil

    class Fert,Soil olive
    class NH3 ochre
    class Aer indigo
    class Clim plum
    classDef indigo fill:#1d4a62,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef plum fill:#48304a,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef olive fill:#5b6e34,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef ochre fill:#d69a2e,stroke:#3b1a18,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#3b1a18
```

An emission inventory replaces the arrow out of the soil with a fixed number, so both loops are cut: deposition cannot raise emission, and climate cannot change it. Most global chemistry–climate models ran this way, with anthropogenic emissions prescribed[^1].

## What was built

The study coupled two components of CESM2[^2]:

| Component | Configuration |
|---|---|
| Land | CLM5 with active carbon–nitrogen cycling and the crop model (CLM5-BGC-Crop) |
| Atmosphere and chemistry | CAM4-chem, MOZART-4 tropospheric chemistry, $1.9^\circ \times 2.5^\circ$, 27 vertical levels |
| Aerosol | a bulk scheme predicting sulfate, nitrate and ammonium in $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ |

Default CLM5 has no ammonia emission at all. The new scheme, adapted from the DNDC model (DeNitrification–DeComposition, version 9.5), computes volatilisation from the soil ammonium pool, the fraction of it adsorbed to clay, soil temperature, soil pH, surface wind speed and the depth of the soil layer. A canopy scheme then recaptures part of the emitted ammonia, depending on leaf area index, wind speed, in-canopy humidity and canopy height. Soil pH is held at $6.5$ everywhere, because CLM5 does not compute it; the authors note that emission is highly sensitive to that choice.

Separate simulations isolate each feedback. Each ran 30 years, with the last 20 analysed:

| Experiment | What it does | Isolates |
|---|---|---|
| Fully coupled, 2000 and 2050 | online emission, online deposition, aerosol–radiation interaction on; 2050 uses $30\%$ more synthetic fertiliser | the total response |
| Prescribed deposition, 2000 and 2050 | online emission, but nitrogen deposition read from a file | the deposition feedback (fully coupled minus this) |
| Prescribed aerosols, 2050 | aerosols and gases in radiation prescribed | the aerosol–climate feedback (fully coupled minus this) |
| Inventory input, 2000 | the CMIP6 inventory instead of online emission | comparison with satellite ammonia (IASI) |

## What the coupled runs found

| Quantity | Result[^2] |
|---|---|
| Fertiliser-induced $\text{NH}_3$ emission, 2000 | $14\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$; inventories give $10$ (CMIP6, EDGAR) and $9.1$ (MASAGE) |
| Global $\text{NH}_3$ change, 2050 versus 2000 | $+3.3\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ ($+24\%$) for a $21\%$ rise in total fertiliser |
| Asian $\text{NH}_3$ change, 2050 versus 2000 | $+1.6\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ ($+24\%$) |
| Deposition feedback: nitrogen deposition | $+1.6\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$, mostly over the US and India |
| Deposition feedback: $\text{NH}_3$ emission | $+0.47\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ |
| Aerosol–climate feedback: $\text{NH}_3$ emission | $-0.41\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$; lower over Africa, higher over India and the Americas |
| Global downward radiative flux, 2050 versus 2000 | $-0.005\text{ W m}^{-2}$ |
| Global grain production, 2050 versus 2000 | $+243\text{ Tg yr}^{-1}$; Europe $+76$ ($+17\%$), North America $+78$ ($+17\%$), Asia $+55$ ($+4\%$) |

Three results matter most.

**Emission responds more than proportionally to fertiliser.** A $21\%$ increase in total fertiliser, from a present-day $96.5\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$, raised emission $24\%$: a super-linear response that a fixed emission factor per kilogram of fertiliser cannot produce.

**The two feedbacks are real but nearly cancel.** Returning deposited nitrogen to the soil adds $0.47\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ of emission; letting aerosols change the climate removes $0.41$. Each is about an eighth of the $3.3\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ fertiliser response ($14\%$ and $12\%$), and they have opposite signs, so globally they nearly cancel. Regionally they do not: the aerosol–climate feedback lowers emission over Africa and raises it over India and the Americas, and the extra deposition falls mostly on the US and India.

**The global radiative effect is negligible.** The $-0.005\text{ W m}^{-2}$ change in downward radiative flux is tiny next to the $-0.27\text{ W m}^{-2}$ multi-model mean anthropogenic aerosol forcing the paper compares it with. The aerosol–climate experiment does show substantial regional surface cooling, but the authors attribute it largely to more dust over sub-Saharan Africa, where dust is computed rather than prescribed, not to fertiliser ammonium.

The authors list the main limitations themselves. Manure management is excluded, though manure may supply up to about $60\%$ of soil ammonia. Emissions are biased high, partly from overly fertile initial soil ammonium, and are especially high over India and the US. Soil pH is fixed. Recaptured canopy ammonia is assumed to return to the soil, which is uncertain. The modified nitrogen oxide scheme was not passed to the atmosphere, and the sulfate indirect effect was not included[^2].

## Key takeaways

- An emission inventory cuts two loops: nitrogen deposited back onto soil cannot raise emission, and aerosol-driven climate change cannot alter it.
- Fung, Val Martin and Tai made fertiliser ammonia an online flux by adding a DNDC-based volatilisation scheme to CLM5 and coupling it to CAM4-chem in CESM2.
- The model attributes $14\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$ of ammonia to fertiliser, above inventories at $9$–$10$, and emission rises $24\%$ for a $21\%$ rise in fertiliser.
- The deposition feedback ($+0.47\text{ Tg N yr}^{-1}$) and the aerosol–climate feedback ($-0.41$) are small and roughly cancel globally; their regional effects differ.
- The global radiative effect is negligible ($-0.005\text{ W m}^{-2}$). The regional cooling in the aerosol experiment comes mostly from dust, not fertiliser aerosol.

## References

[^1]: Lamarque, J.-F. et al. The Atmospheric Chemistry and Climate Model Intercomparison Project (ACCMIP): overview and description of models, simulations and climate diagnostics. *Geosci. Model Dev.* **6**, 179–206 (2013). https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-6-179-2013
[^2]: Fung, K. M., Val Martin, M. & Tai, A. P. K. Modeling the interinfluence of fertilizer-induced $\text{NH}_3$ emission, nitrogen deposition, and aerosol radiative effects using modified CESM2. *Biogeosciences* **19**, 1635–1655 (2022). https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-19-1635-2022
